newsitem.title: UK: Softs outlook-Volatile coffee should hold limelight.
newsitem.headline: Softs outlook-Volatile coffee should hold limelight.

text.p: Robusta coffee's volatility should act as focus for London's soft commodity markets this week, while an approaching New York expiry is likely to set the tone for white sugar, traders said on Monday.
Cocoa remains trapped in the shadow of a long-term downtrend, prone to the vagaries of currency movements.
Robusta futures, still languishing behind the pace of the New York market, are expected to retain their recent volatility with May prices fluctuating widely between $1,450 and $1,700 a tonne.
But traders said industry buyers would be lured by robusta coffee's hefty discount to New York arabicas and underpin the downside potential of the London market.
One major concern arising from this year's price hike is the potential effect on world coffee consumption.
"The last time we had the price hike after the (1994) Brazilian frosts, people underestimated the impact on consumption," one trader said.
But he added that the market outlook should not be seen in too negative a light in the longer term.
"I think London will hold relatively well further into the year," he said. "Obviously that doesn't take into account the weather revenge."
Traders said the size of Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop would provide the real key to market direction.

Even with 25 million bags there would not be sufficient coffee to meet demand, they said, noting that with roasters' current hand-to-mouth buying policy any disruption to supplies would make the market nervous.
In sugar, traders said attention would centre on New York where spot March is set to expire on Friday.

Although London has been correcting lower after last week's rally -- a reaction to a fund-led buying spree in New York -- white values could remain strong while the March raws remained on the board, they said.
"I do think it (London) is too high but I don't think it'll come down until after March expires, unless we get something fundamentally new," said one.
Arbitrage activity has recently been more of a function of the sharp movements in both markets than actual trading.
On the raws market, the expected strength in March could drag May higher and thus cause May/May to narrow amid the background of rumoured supply tightness in key producers Brazil and Cuba, he said.
But despite the higher futures prices more physical buyers have emerged, mainly from the Middle East.
Cocoa traders said the London market needed a fresh dose of fundamental news to kick it out of the currency-dominated stupor which set last week's quiet tone.
Nearby values have recently been trapped in a sideways consolidation move, in the longer-term background of a downtrend in place since last August.
"The possibilities of our shaking the market free are slim," said one trader, but suggested that purchases in Ghana or Ivory Coast could provide such a signal.
Despite last week's marginal tail-off, Ghana cocoa purchases showed the global deficit was likely to be smaller than earlier estimates, he said.
"I think the majority would now say the deficit is going to be smaller than they once thought," he said.
According to ICCO data, the world cocoa deficit is forecast at 225,000 tonnes for 1996/97 (Oct/Sept), compared with a 1995/96 surplus of 133,000 tonnes.
Market players are thought to be looking for a much more manageable figure of 100,000 tonnes, or lower, and thinking in terms of a small deficit for next season.
Technical analysts said while the benchmark May contract appeared to be bottoming out between 870 and 880 stg, it needed to break above 900 to confirm an uptrend.
